title: Audit telemetry, KMS & on-prem export walkthrough - Lacerta Finance
header:
Date: 2025-12-22
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: enabled
Attendees: Jordan Miles, Priya Anand, Liam O'Connor (Redwood); Evelyn Park, Marcus Holt, Sana Riaz, Tomás Alvarez (Lacerta Finance)
summary: High-level walkthrough of Redwood audit telemetry: what admin activity and request logs capture, off-platform export options (S3, syslog, Kafka), retention defaults and configurable TTLs, KMS/CMEK models, on-prem export patterns for air-gapped environments, and integration points with Splunk/Sumo. Agreed next steps include trialing a 90-day export to Lacerta's S3, providing SOC2 evidence pack and key rotation docs, and a short PO C for on-prem collector in January.
topics: What audit logs capture (admin vs request-level)
Export options: S3, syslog, Kafka, webhook streaming
Retention defaults and policy (30/90/365), legal hold
Encryption at rest & in transit, KMS/CMEK/HSM
On-prem export and air-gapped collector design
SIEM integrations (Splunk, Sumo, Datadog) and schema
Redaction and PII handling in logs
Access controls and RBAC around audit views
transcript: [00:00:05] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:00:12] Evelyn: Evelyn here from Lacerta, Hi.
[00:00:15] Marcus: Marcus on the call, Platform.
[00:00:18] Sana: Sana, compliance.
[00:00:22] Priya: Priya—security SE at Redwood. I'll lead the tech portions re: logs and KMS.
[00:00:30] Jordan: We scheduled 50 minutes. Goal is to make sure our audit telemetry meets your SOC 2 needs and show export options for your retention policy.
[00:00:45] Tomás: Quick ask up front — we need an on-prem option or a V P C export; customer data residency is non negotiable for some flows.
[00:00:55] Priya: Totally, we'll cover on‑prem collectors, VPC egress to your S3, and a syslog/ Kafka pipeline. We'll also talk about CMEK — customer managed encryption keys.

[00:01:12] Jordan: Quick framing: Redwood splits telemetry into two main buckets — admin activity (console/API admin ops) and request-level events (model requests, tokens, routing decisions). We'll show examples of both.
[00:01:30] Marcus: When you say request-level, does that include prompt text? We need to know about PII and redaction.

[00:01:38] Priya: Good question — by default request payloads that are user content are not stored in the admin audit index in plain text. We capture metadata: request id, model id, route, latency, token counts, and hashes for traceability. Full payloads can be retained if you opt in for debugging — we mark that as sensitive and store behind CMEK with role-based access. There's also configurable on-the-fly redaction for common PII patterns (ssn, credit card, email) but it's regex-based and not perfect.
[00:02:10] Sana: So for SOC 2 evidence we need immutable admin logs for changes (user create/delete, role changes). Are those exports tamper-evident?

[00:02:18] Priya: Admin events are append-only and signed at rest with HMAC; when exported to S3 we include an audit manifest with checksums. For high-assurance we also support streaming to an HSM-backed SIEM where events are timestamped and chained — basically tamper-evident.
[00:02:40] Marcus: You mentioned manifest and checksums — do you support object lock on S3 for retention/immutable buckets?

[00:02:47] Priya: Yes, customers can configure our export to write into a bucket that has S3 Object Lock / WORM. Redwood will not delete or mutate exported files; it's a push-only system. You need to give the export role write-only to the bucket.
[00:03:05] Evelyn: What's the default retention on the platform itself?

[00:03:09] Jordan: On the hosted product we keep admin audit events for 90 days by default, request level metadata for 30 days. We offer configurable tiers: 30, 90, 365, or custom via Dedicated/Private. Many enterprise customers choose to export daily to their S3 and configure their own multi-year retention.
[00:03:30] Tomás: If we export daily, is there any chance of missing events due to platform outages?

[00:03:35] Priya: We buffer locally and retry; we also keep a 7-day replay window for exports in case of transient failures. For on-prem collectors you can point to a Kafka cluster to ensure high durability.
[00:03:50] Marcus: How does the export look — CSV, JSON, newline-delimited JSON? We have parsers in Splunk expecting ndjson with a specific schema.

[00:03:58] Priya: Exports are ndjson; schema doc will be provided. Each event has top-level fields: timestamp, event_type, principal, resource, action, request_id, model_variant, latency_ms, token_counts, and an optional payload_hash. We also include an event_version to support schema evolution. We'll send the spec after the call.
[00:04:20] Sana: For compliance we must show who viewed admin logs. Is there RBAC on the audit viewer UI?

[00:04:26] Liam: Yes — RBAC is integrated. Audit viewers are a distinct role; we track audit viewer access as an admin event too, so you can prove who accessed logs and when. We can also push those access events into your SIEM.
[00:04:45] Evelyn: KMS — do you support our KMS in AWS (CMEK), or do we have to use Redwood's keys?

[00:04:51] Priya: For Private deployments you can bring your own KMS via AWS KMS or GCP KMS. For Hosted we offer optional CMEK where keys live in your cloud project and Redwood uses a short-lived wrapping key. We also integrate with HSM for Dedicated if you need FIPS/HSM attestation. There's a small operational overhead for rotation, which we automate if you allow it.
[00:05:20] Marcus: Rotation — how do you handle rolling keys when logs are encrypted?

[00:05:24] Priya: We use envelope encryption. Data is encrypted with a data key, which is wrapped by the KMS key. When rotating, we re-wrap existing data keys and write a new manifest entry. For exported files we include key metadata so your on-prem SIEM can access or validate as long as you maintain key access.
[00:05:45] Tomás: Air-gapped on-prem — what's the pattern?

[00:05:49] Priya: Two patterns: 1) On-prem collector: a small shim that runs in your network, pulls telemetry from a private control-plane endpoint over mutual TLS, and writes to local S3 or syslog, 2) Full Private install: Redwood stack inside your VPC/on-prem that keeps all telemetry local. The shim supports periodic manual transfer for fully air-gapped networks.
[00:06:12] Marcus: Can the collector sign events with our HSM?
[00:06:16] Priya: Yes, the collector can integrate with your HSM to sign events before writing them to storage. That gives you local chain of custody.
[00:06:25] Sana: For SOC 2 we need a clear chain of custody and retention policy. Is there an out-of-the-box evidence pack?

[00:06:30] Jordan: We maintain an evidence pack that includes exported audit manifests, role change logs, access proofs, and policy screenshots. We'll provide the SOC2 evidence bundle; however customers often augment with their own SIEM extracts. We'll attach the redacted example in the follow-up.
[00:06:50] Marcus: Are there rate limits on exports? We have very high throughput during batch jobs.

[00:06:55] Priya: Export is throttled by default to avoid overwhelming customer endpoints but we can provision higher throughput on Dedicated plans. For S3 push we do multipart uploads and parallelize. For Kafka we support partitioning.
[00:07:10] Evelyn: Legal hold — if we need to keep a subset of events for an investigation beyond the normal TTL, how's that done?

[00:07:15] Priya: There is a legal hold API; you mark a query or a set of request_ids — Redwood keeps those events immutable and prevents purging until the hold is removed. Exports will include those marked events with a hold flag.
[00:07:28] Tomás: What about redact-on-export vs redact-in-platform? Which one do you recommend?

[00:07:33] Priya: If compliance needs you should redact at export time — that way your downstream SIEM never sees PII. But if you need full fidelity for debugging, keep a secure CMEK-protected debug bucket with strictly limited access. So it's often both: redacted stream for analytics, full debug bucket under strict controls.
[00:07:52] Marcus: Does Redwood capture KV cache access patterns or only model request metadata? We need to detect abuse of cache keys.

[00:07:58] Priya: We log cache events (cache hits/misses, evictions) as part of request telemetry with a cache_key_hash rather than raw keys. That gives you observability without exposing internal keys.
[00:08:12] Jordan: Switching to integrations — what SIEMs do you support?

[00:08:16] Priya: Out-of-the-box we have connectors for Splunk HEC, Sumo Logic, Datadog, and generic syslog/HTTPS webhooks. For Splunk we can deliver ndjson to HEC and provide a sample Splunk query and dashboard. We'll share a Splunk ingestion sample.
[00:08:32] Sana: Splunk is our main SIEM — can you preserve event ordering? Important for forensic timelines.

[00:08:37] Priya: We include event sequence numbers and strongly-ordered timestamps. For streaming exports like Kafka or HEC we'll provide a partitioning key (request_id % partitions) to keep ordering per request. There are caveats under heavy load but we'll discuss SLA for ordering.
[00:08:57] Marcus: On retention: you said 90 days default. If we need 7 years for certain logs, do we need Dedicated or Private?

[00:09:04] Jordan: For multi-year retention customers almost always export to their own storage where they control retention. Dedicated can be configured to store long-term too but most prefer S3/archival for cost efficiency.
[00:09:15] Evelyn: Can you show an example exported event?

[00:09:18] Priya: (screen shares) Here's an ndjson line: {timestamp:..., event_type: "admin:role.update", principal: "evelyn@lacerta.com", resource: "project-23", action: "role_change", request_id: "r-abc123", details: {before: "viewer", after: "admin"}, hash: "sha256:..."} — note in real export the details may be redacted or hashed depending on settings.
[00:09:46] Marcus: The transcription missed colons there — but I get the point. How do you ensure the exported files are tamper-evident for auditors?

[00:09:52] Priya: Each file has a SHA256 checksum in the manifest, and we can optionally PGP-sign the manifest. For deeper assurance we offer an append-only ledger service that chains file entries (like a merkle chain) and we can provide attestation logs.
[00:10:10] Tomás: Do you have any examples of customers using Object Lock and Glacier for long retention?
[00:10:15] Jordan: Yes, financial customers typically export to S3 with Object Lock enabled and lifecycle to Glacier for older data. That's standard practice. We'll share anonymized case studies.
[00:10:26] Sana: On SSO and RBAC — if someone leaves the company, how does deprovisioning reflect in audit logs?

[00:10:32] Liam: Deprovisioning events are immediate admin events. We also recommend SCIM integration for automatic personnel sync. In the evidence pack you'll see user.delete events and linked session termination events.
[00:10:45] Marcus: For our legal/compliance team, we need to show the chain from console action to API call to exported file. Is that traceable?

[00:10:52] Priya: Yes, every action has a request_id that is propagated through the system and included in export. The manifest maps request_id -> file path -> checksum. That allows forensic reconstruction.
[00:11:05] Evelyn: Anything special for GDPR or data residency?

[00:11:09] Priya: We support region-specific deployments and data residency controls. For hosted, you can pin region for data at rest. For regulated workloads we recommend Private deployments or Dedicated capacity to ensure all telemetry remains in your region.
[00:11:22] Marcus: We're also interested in alerting on suspicious admin activity — is that part of telemetry?

[00:11:27] Priya: We have built-in alerting rules (login anomalies, role escalations, unusual export patterns). Alerts can be pushed to your PagerDuty, Slack, or SIEM as events. You can tune thresholds. We'll share a sample rule pack.
[00:11:45] Tomás: Any cost implication for storing debug payloads?
[00:11:49] Jordan: Yes — storing full payloads has cost and privacy implications. We price debug payload storage separately and recommend lifecycle policies to move to cheaper storage after X days.
[00:11:58] Sana: For the SOC 2 audit we'll need to demonstrate separation of duties — e.g., who can flip the export config?

[00:12:04] Priya: Changing export config is an admin action that requires the owner role. All attempts are logged and require two-step confirmation for Dedicated customers if you enable stricter controls.
[00:12:18] Marcus: Does Redwood provide an API for ad-hoc exports if we need a specific timeframe for an eDiscovery?
[00:12:23] Priya: Yes — ad-hoc exports via the Audit API. You can query by time range, principal, request_id and request a signed archive. There is an approval flow for production exports.
[00:12:35] Evelyn: Let's talk timelines. We want to run a POC for on‑prem collector in January. What's realistic?
[00:12:41] Jordan: Realistic: 2–4 weeks to stand up a collector in a dev environment with your infra team. For a hardened air-gapped flow add 4–6 weeks. We'll scope it in the next step.
[00:12:52] Marcus: Are there known limitations with encrypted exports and cross-account access? We use separate AWS accounts for logs.

[00:12:58] Priya: We support cross-account S3 write with AssumeRole. The export manifest contains the target account ID. For CMEK you'll need to provide key policies to allow Redwood's export role to wrap keys — we document the exact IAM/CMEK policy.
[00:13:15] Tomás: Any gotchas with key rotation and archived exports? Suppose we rotate keys yearly but need to decrypt a file from 3 years ago.

[00:13:22] Priya: As long as you retain the old KMS master key material or ensure key history retained in AWS KMS, you can re-wrap data keys. If you use a true HSM with key destruction policies you must be careful. We'll include recommended key retention guidance.
[00:13:40] Sana: Can Redwood redact logs before export using a DLP engine?

[00:13:44] Priya: We have a light DLP/redaction engine built-in that does pattern-based masking. For advanced needs we support integrating with customer DLP via webhook to perform on-the-fly redaction before writing to your endpoint. That's part of the Dedicated/Private feature set.
[00:14:02] Marcus: I need to know about retention enforcement. If we accidentally delete an S3 object, do you keep a copy?

[00:14:08] Priya: Redwood does not keep additional copies of exported files beyond what you configure. For stronger guarantees keep a copy in Glacier or use cross-region replication. For short replay windows we have a 7-day buffer but it's not a long-term backup.
[00:14:22] Jordan: Quick poll — who needs the SOC2 evidence pack and KMS rotation docs in the next 48 hours?
[00:14:28] Evelyn: Yes, we do.
[00:14:30] Sana: Please.
[00:14:32] Marcus: Also sample Splunk ingestion config.
[00:14:35] Priya: We'll attach all three: evidence pack, KMS rotation guide, Splunk HEC sample. Also the ndjson schema.
[00:14:42] Tomás: One more question — do you capture changes to model routing policies? We need to know if a policy switch happened that could affect responses.
[00:14:49] Priya: Yes, policy changes are admin events and include before/after snapshots. We also include rollout metadata (canary percentage, timestamp).
[00:15:02] Marcus: Any specific logging for function/tool-calling or tool outputs?

[00:15:08] Priya: Tool invocations are logged as events; outputs can be redacted. We typically log metadata (tool_name, duration, success/fail) and a hash of result if you need traceability without content.
[00:15:25] Jordan: We're about halfway through — want to open up for any questions on specifics?
[00:15:30] Evelyn: Quick one: SLA on exports — can you guarantee delivery within X minutes?

[00:15:35] Priya: For Hosted exports we target delivery within 15 minutes and a 99.5% per-file success rate. For high-throughput Dedicated we can tighten that. We'll provide an export SLA in the contract addendum.
[00:15:50] Sana: For auditors we need samples of both redacted and full debug exports. Can you provide anonymized examples?
[00:15:55] Jordan: Yes — we'll provide anonymized samples.
[00:16:02] Marcus: Any known limitations with EU region and cross-border key management?

[00:16:07] Priya: If you require keys to never leave the region you must use our Private deployment or a regional KMS with CMEK configured in that region. Hosted CMEK will respect region constraints but double-check the key policy. We'll include regional deployment notes.
[00:16:25] Tomás: How are entry points authenticated? mTLS?
[00:16:29] Priya: Collector uses mutual TLS and short-lived certs. API calls are authenticated with short-lived tokens; exports to S3 use signed AssumeRole credentials.
[00:16:38] Marcus: Can we run the collector in an ephemeral container as part of our infra?
[00:16:42] Priya: Yes, we provide a docker image and helm chart for Kubernetes. The collector can be run as a cron job or long-lived service. We'll share the helm values.
[00:16:52] Sana: Anything else we should be aware of re: audit log fidelity?

[00:16:56] Priya: Two caveats: 1) If you enable aggressive sampling on request payloads for cost control you lose some fidelity; 2) client-side redaction before reaching Redwood is final — we don't have the original payload. We'll document these trade-offs.
[00:17:12] Jordan: Let's move to next steps and wrap. I'll summarize.

[00:17:15] Jordan: Actions: Redwood to share SOC2 evidence pack, KMS rotation doc, Splunk ingestion sample; Lacerta to provision an S3 bucket for test exports and share the role; schedule on-prem collector POC for week of Jan 13. Any objections?
[00:17:30] Evelyn: Sounds good.
[00:17:33] Marcus: OK.
[00:17:35] Sana: Agree.
[00:17:37] Tomás: Fine.

[00:17:40] Jordan: End notes: we'll also include a short checklist for auditors showing where to find user.delete, role.change, export manifests. We'll also include a short demo recording snippet for the Splunk demo.
[00:17:52] Priya: And I'll assign an SE to the POC — likely Liam. I'll also ping with the ndjson schema and a sample pipeline script for S3->Splunk ingestion.
[00:18:05] Liam: Happy to run the POC with Tomás. I'll put a proposed plan in the next steps.
[00:18:12] Jordan: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up by EOD with docs. Meeting end.
